name: Exclamative Clause

dimensions.form: Tensed Clause headed by a VP and marked by an exclamative phrase based on what or how; normally the exclamative phrase is initial and Subject precedes the Predicator
dimensions.meaning: Presents a proposition as holding to a remarkable degree or in a remarkable way relative to a contextual norm
dimensions.function: Characteristically makes an exclamatory statement, without being identical to the broader pragmatic category of exclamation
dimensions.distribution: Main clauses and subordinate exclamative content clauses

1.definition: A headed clause type marked by an exclamative what/how phrase and characteristically used for an exclamatory statement
1.details: Exclamative what and how mark clause type while also performing a core role inside the exclamative phrase. Headed exclamatives are normally tensed and usually have Subject–Predicator order, although subject postposing and subject–auxiliary inversion are possible. Clause type must be kept distinct from force: exclamative is one syntactic source of exclamatory statements, while the wider exclamation profile also includes interjections, NPs, and recruited declaratives. Phrase-only What a disaster! is not a headed Clause in this project and belongs with clause-analogue semantics (CGEL pp. 853–57, 918–23).

examples.form: I realised [what a bargain it was].
[How happy would he be if he could see her once more!]
examples.note: Marked but licensed subject–auxiliary inversion in a headed exclamative

constraints.description: The construction is a Clause headed by VP and contains an exclamative phrase based on what or how; Subject–Predicator order is usual but not invariant.
A phrase-only expression such as What a disaster! is not an instance of this headed construction; its clausal interpretation belongs under clause-analogue-001.
Exclamatory statement is the characteristic use, but exclamative clause type is not coextensive with exclamation or with exclamatory prosody.

projection.target: An exclamative what/how phrase inside a headed Clause predicts remarkable-degree interpretation, a strong preference for Subject–Predicator order, and availability in both main and subordinate exclamative environments
projection.evidence: What/how marking covaries with evaluative degree semantics across main and subordinate headed clauses, while the order possibilities distinguish this construction from open interrogatives without defining it by punctuation or force

grounds.note: Exclamative marking projects remarkable-degree interpretation and main/subordinate distribution
The form-meaning-order profile recurs across headed exclamatives

relatedConstructions.notes: Exclamative what/how supplies both a core phrasal role and the feature marking the Clause as exclamative
Exclamative clauses characteristically realize exclamatory force, but the pragmatic exclamation profile is broader than this clause type
What and how can mark either type, but role, order, meaning, and context distinguish them
Phrase-only exclamatory expressions receive clausal interpretations without being headed Clauses

grounds.note: Exclamative clause marking, syntax, characteristic meaning, and distinction from the wider class of exclamations

curious.title: What and how sentences of surprise
curious.summary: Some sentences start with what or how to present something as remarkable.
curious.body:
What a fine player she is! and How generous you are! both present something as remarkable, as measured against what we'd expect. Each starts with a what or how phrase, then normally the person or thing, then the verb.

These are clauses, meaning groups of words built around a verb. They can stand alone, as above, or sit inside a bigger sentence: I realised what a bargain it was. The usual order can change, as in How happy would he be if he could see her once more!, which is a marked but allowed pattern. A phrase with no verb, such as What a disaster!, isn't counted here.

examples.text: I realised [what a bargain it was].
[How happy would he be if he could see her once more!]

curious.try: Make your own sentence that starts with What a or How. Where does the verb come, before or after the person or thing?

teacher.summary: Helps students recognize what and how exclamatives as verb-headed clauses, and tell them from questions and from phrase-only exclamations.
teacher.explain: An exclamative clause is a clause headed by a VP (normally tensed) and marked by an exclamative phrase based on what or how. It presents a proposition as holding to a remarkable degree or in a remarkable way, and characteristically makes an exclamatory statement. The exclamative phrase is normally initial and the Subject precedes the Predicator, though subject postposing and subject-auxiliary inversion are possible. It occurs in main clauses and as a subordinate content clause. Clause type isn't the same as force: exclamation is a wider pattern of use. Phrase-only What a disaster! isn't a headed clause in this dictionary; see the clause-analogue entry. What and how can also mark open interrogatives, and role, order, meaning and context separate the two.
teacher.terms: Exclamative clause is CGEL's term. Sentences like these are sometimes called exclamatory sentences.

examples.text: I realised [what a bargain it was].
[How happy would he be if he could see her once more!]

watch_for: A learner might treat any sentence beginning with what or how as an exclamative, when the same words can start an open interrogative.
A learner might take Subject-Predicator order as required, though the how-happy example shows a licensed inversion.
A learner might count What a disaster! as a verb-headed clause, when this dictionary treats it as phrase-only.
teacher.activity: Students get strips with what/how sentences, some exclamatives and some questions (What did she play? alongside What a fine player she is!). They sort them and mark where the verb and subject fall.

child.hook: Which sentence shows surprise, What a fine player she is or What did she play?
child.explain: Some sentences start with What a or How to show something is remarkable. What a fine player she is!
child.play: Look at a picture. Say something amazing about it that starts with What a or How.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body and teacher.explain no longer make tense part of what a clause is or require it (the entry says headed exclamatives are normally tensed); child.explain no longer states subject-before-verb order as a rule (the entry allows subject postposing and inversion); curious.body says normally for the order.
